subject: DOC
front: Which Greek word denoting lordship was most frequently used of Jesus, and what did it invite?
back: Kurios - "The Lord" or "The Master". To use this name invited opposition from the Jewish authorities on the grounds of blasphemy, and from the Romans on the grounds of treason against the Emperor.
excerpt: The most requent, and the most important in relation to the doctrine of his person, was the Greek word kurios, spoken of him as "The Lord" or "The Master."

subject: DOC
front: What is Arianism, and after whom is it named?
back: The heresy which denies Christ's divinity, named after Arius of Alexandria (died 335). Arius taught that the Son of God and the Holy Spirit were beings willed into existence by God for the purposes of redemption, so that they were not eternal: there was a time "before which they were not".
excerpt: The heresy of the denial of Christ's divinity usually goes by the name of Arianism (after Arius of Alexandria; died 335).

subject: DOC
front: What is Docetism, and from what Greek word does it come?
back: The heresy which denies Christ's humanity. From the Greek verb dokeo, "to appear" or "to seem": Jesus only seemed to be a man, his human nature being a mask concealing his true divine self.
excerpt: The word Docetism comes from the Greek verb dokeo which means "to appear" or "to seem."

subject: DOC
front: What are the technical names for the doctrine of Christ's person and the doctrine of Christ's work?
back: Christology (the person of Christ) and soteriology (the work of Christ). The person and work of Christ are inseparable.
excerpt: the doctrines of Christ's person (Christology) pass quickly and inevitably into the area of Christ's work (soteriology)

subject: DOC
front: What are the "tenses" of salvation?
back: We have been saved from the penalty of sin by a crucified Saviour; we are being saved from the power of sin by a living Saviour; we shall be saved from the presence of sin by a coming Saviour.
excerpt: The "tenses" of salvation are as follows: we have been saved from the penalty of sin by a crucified Saviour; we are being saved from the power of sin by a living Saviour; we shall be saved from the presence of sin by a coming Saviour.

subject: DOC
front: What is the threefold office of Christ?
back: Prophet, priest and king. As prophet he is the perfect spokesman of God; as priest he offered a sufficient sacrifice and now intercedes; as king he is "the ruler over the kings of the earth".
excerpt: The work of Christ has often been stated in relation to his threefold office as prophet, priest, and king.

subject: DOC
front: What factual evidence for the resurrection does the syllabus give?
back: The empty tomb containing only the abandoned grave clothes; the persistent failure of all explanations other than that Christ had risen; and the numerous reported appearances of the risen Jesus at different times and before different people.
excerpt: There is the empty tomb, containing only the abandoned grave clothes, and the persistent failure of all explanations other than that Christ had risen.

subject: DOC
front: Why did the sinless Jesus submit to John's baptism of repentance?
back: By his submission to John's baptism he showed his identification with sinful humanity; the descent of the Spirit like a dove and the Father's words of acceptance came as God's approval of the ministry that was to follow.
excerpt: Jesus, however, had no sin of which he could repent. But by his submission to John's baptism, he showed his identification with sinful humanity.

subject: DOC
topic: The Deity of the Holy Spirit
front: What is the place of the Holy Spirit in the Godhead?
back: He is the third person of the Trinity, presented in the Bible as a person fully worthy of worship.
excerpt: The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Trinity (Matt. 28:19; 2 Cor. 13:14). He is presented in the Bible as a person fully worthy of worship.

subject: DOC
topic: The Deity of the Holy Spirit
front: Which divine attributes does the syllabus ascribe to the Holy Spirit?
back: Holy, Eternal (Heb. 9:14), Omnipotent (Gen. 1:2; Job 26:13), Omniscient (1 Cor. 2:10, 11), Omnipresent (Ps. 139:7-10) and Truth (1 John 5:6).
excerpt: Eternal 		-	Hebrews 9:14

subject: DOC
topic: The Person of the Holy Spirit
front: What five characteristics show that the Holy Spirit is a living, self-conscious person?
back: He has Knowledge; He has Intelligence; He has Emotion; He Acts; and He has Will Power (the Spirit makes decisions).
excerpt:
The Holy Spirit is a living being who is self-conscious and therefore, 
has the following characteristics:

subject: DOC
front: What are the five names of the Holy Spirit given in the syllabus?
back: The Holy Spirit; The Spirit of God; The Spirit of Christ; The Spirit of Truth; and The Counsellor or Helper.
excerpt: The Holy Spirit: The third person of the Trinity is best known by this name.

subject: DOC
front: What is the literal meaning of the name "Counsellor"?
back: One who comes alongside. The name is reassuring for Christians facing temptation, doubt, demanding service or opposition.
excerpt: The literal meaning of the term "Counsellor" is one who comes alongside.

subject: DOC
topic: The Emblems of the Holy Spirit
front: What are the six emblems of the Holy Spirit?
back: Wind, Water, Fire, Oil, the Dove and a Seal. They throw light upon both his nature and his mission.
excerpt:
Wind: Wind here indicates unseen power, and the main ideas conveyed are mystery, 
sovereignty and energy.

subject: DOC
topic: The Emblems of the Holy Spirit
front: What five things does the emblem of Fire indicate?
back: The presence of the Lord; the protection of the Lord; the approval of the Lord; the purifying from the Lord; and the judgment of the Lord.
excerpt: the presence of the Lord (Ex. 3:2)

subject: DOC
topic: The Emblems of the Holy Spirit
front: What does the emblem of a Seal indicate?
back: Ownership, finished transaction, identification, security, value, authority and genuineness.
excerpt: A seal indicates ownership, finished transaction, identification, security, value, authority, genuineness

subject: DOC
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
front: What are the nine elements of the fruit of the Spirit?
back: Love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (Gal. 5:22-23). Note that "fruit" is singular: there are not nine fruits but one fruit of nine elements, namely Christ-likeness.
excerpt: "The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such, there is no law" (Gal. 5:22-23).

subject: DOC
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
front: What six things does the Holy Spirit do in the life of the Christian?
back: Life (new birth by the Spirit); Assurance (the witness of the Spirit); Unity (fellowship in the Spirit); Ownership (the seal of the Spirit); Power (the fullness of the Spirit); and Confidence (the pledge of the Spirit).
excerpt: From the beginning of Christian discipleship, the Holy Spirit lives within the Christian. He gives the Christian the power to follow Christ, confidence in believing, and unity with other Christians.

subject: DOC
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
front: How did Archbishop William Temple describe the Holy Spirit?
back: "First and foremost the special and distinctive influence which God exerts over our souls as we respond to his love in the human life of Christ."
excerpt: Thus the late Archbishop William Temple described the Holy Spirit as "first and foremost the special and distinctive influence which God exerts over our souls as we respond to his love in the human life of Christ."

subject: DOC
topic: The Work of the Holy Spirit
front: What are spiritual gifts?
back: Supernatural abilities given by the Holy Spirit to believers. After the Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost he began his ministry of gift-giving, and will continue till Christ comes again.
excerpt: Spiritual gifts are supernatural abilities given by the Holy Spirit to believers.

subject: DOC
topic: Hallmark of the Gifts of the Spirit
front: Which four passages of Scripture list some of the gifts of the Holy Spirit?
back: Romans 12:6-8; 1 Corinthians 12:8-10; Ephesians 4:11, 12; and 1 Peter 4:10, 11.
excerpt: Four passages of Scripture list some of the gifts: Roman. 12:6-8; 1 Corinthians 12:8-10; Ephesians 4:11, 12; 1 Peter 4:10, 11.

subject: DOC
front: Who formulated the doctrine of the Trinity, and when was it proclaimed as the faith of the Church?
back: Early Church Fathers such as Irenaeus, Origen and Tertullian were responsible for the formulation. Under the leadership of Bishop Athanasius it was proclaimed as the faith of the Church at the Council of Nicaea in AD 325, and a century later, at the hands of Bishop Augustine, it was accepted by Trinitarian churches.
excerpt: Early Church Fathers such as Irenaeus, Origen and Tertullian were responsible for the formulation of the doctrine.

subject: DOC
topic: Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity)
front: What is Modalism?
back: The view that the one God assumes different forms, or plays different roles: first Creator and Law-giver, then Redeemer, then the Holy Spirit who is Enlightener and Sanctifier.
excerpt: Modalism: This view teaches that the one God assumes different forms, or plays different roles.

subject: DOC
topic: Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity)
front: What is Tri-Theism?
back: The teaching which presents the three persons of the Godhead as consisting of three separate (but co-operating) Gods. It emphasises the Three-ness of God but overlooks the Oneness, the indivisible unity of God.
excerpt: Tri-Theism: This teaching pictures and presents the three persons of the Godhead (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) as consisting of three separate (but co-operating) Gods.

subject: DOC
topic: Some Heresies (False Views about the Trinity)
front: How did William Barclay answer Modalism?
back: "God is always, from eternity (before time), through time, and when time shall end, Creator, Redeemer, Sustainer and Enlightener." A. Wainwright adds, "God redeems through Christ in the power of the Holy Spirit."
excerpt: As William Barclay emphasizes, "God is always, from eternity (before time), through time, and when time shall end, Creator, Redeemer, Sustainer and Enlightener."

subject: DOC
front: How do the Westminster and Belgic Confessions state the doctrine of the Trinity?
back: Westminster: "In the unity of the Godhead there are three persons of one substance, power, and eternity." Belgic: "God is one in essence, yet distinguished in three persons."
excerpt: The Belgic Confession says the same thing: "God is one in essence, yet distinguished in three persons."

subject: DOC
front: Are there three persons or personalities in God?
back: No. "There are not three persons or personalities in God. God is only one person" - the one person who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, having three distinct "ways of existence" simultaneously, not in temporal succession.
excerpt: It is very important to note that there are not three persons or personalities in God. God is only one person.

subject: DOC
topic: The Biblical Source of the Doctrine of the Trinity
front: Does the Bible teach the doctrine of the Trinity?
back: No. Neither the word "trinity" nor language such as "three persons" or "one substance" is biblical language; it is the language of the ancient Church, taken from classical Greek philosophy. But the roots of the doctrine are found in Scripture.
excerpt: The Bible does not teach the doctrine of the Trinity.

subject: DOC
topic: The Biblical Source of the Doctrine of the Trinity
front: What two expressions does Robert Culver give for the inner relations within the Godhead?
back: The eternal generation of the Son by the Father; and the eternal aspiration (or procession) of the Spirit from the Father and the Son.
excerpt: The eternal generation of the Son by the Father; and

subject: DOC
front: How does J.N.D. Kelly define a creed?
back: "A creed is a fixed formula that summarizes the essential articles of the Christian religion and enjoys the sanction of ecclesiastical authority."
excerpt: According to J.N.D. Kelly, "A creed is a fixed formula that summarizes the essential articles of the Christian religion and enjoys the sanction of ecclesiastical authority."

subject: DOC
front: By whom and when was the Nicene Creed adopted and revised?
back: Adopted by the First Council of Nicaea (AD 325), convened by the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great (ruled AD 306-337), and revised by the First Council of Constantinople (AD 381). Nicaea rejected Arianism and proclaimed the divinity and equality of Jesus Christ in the Trinity.
excerpt: This is a creed adopted by the First Council of Nicaea (AD. 325) and revised by the First Council of Constantinople (AD. 381).

subject: DOC
front: What is the Athanasian Creed?
back: A Christian creed originating in Europe in the fourth century, relating especially to the doctrines of the Trinity and the bodily incarnation of Christ. It was originally ascribed to Saint Athanasius, but is now believed to be the work of an unknown writer of the time.
excerpt: A Christian Creed originating in Europe in the fourth century and relating especially to the doctrines of the Trinity and the bodily incarnation of Christ.

subject: DOC
topic: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed
front: Who was Arius and what did he teach?
back: A presbyter from Alexandria. He said the Son (Jesus Christ) was a creature and not God: only God the Father is unbegotten and self-subsistent, the Son is begotten, so there must have been a time when he was not.
excerpt: One of those who attempted to give an answer was Arius, a presbyter from Alexandria. He said the Son (Jesus Christ) was a creature and not God.

subject: DOC
topic: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed
front: Who opposed Arius and suspended him from office?
back: Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria.
excerpt: This view was strongly opposed by Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, who suspended Arius from office.

subject: DOC
topic: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed
front: What is homoousios, and where was it enshrined?
back: "Of the same being" or "consubstantial" - the most accurate term the church could find to express the relation of Christ to the Father. It was enshrined by the ecumenical council at Constantinople in 381, which agreed what we now call the Nicene Creed (more accurately the Niceno-Constantinopolitan creed).
excerpt: It enshrined the word homoousios, "of the same being" or "consubstantial", as the most accurate term the church could find to express the relation of Christ to the Father.

subject: DOC
topic: History of the Formulation of the Nicene Creed
front: What is the Filioque?
back: The Latin expression for the words "and the Son", added in the West under the influence of St. Augustine of Hippo, so that the Creed reads that the Holy Spirit "proceeds from the Father and the Son". The Eastern Church preferred to say "from the Father through the Son".
excerpt: This new addition was captured in the popular Latin expression Filioque.

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
front: From what Greek words does "church" derive, and what is the doctrine of the church called?
back: From kyriake ("belonging to the Lord") and ekklesia ("assembly"). The doctrine of the church is "ecclesiology".
excerpt: The word "church" derives from the Greek kyriake ("belonging to the Lord") and ekklesia ("assembly").

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
front: What is the difference between the Church Militant and the Church Triumphant?
back: Those still in this world, fighting the battle on earth and not yet called home to heaven, constitute the Church Militant; those who battled on earth and have been called home to heaven constitute the Church Triumphant.
excerpt: Those who are still in this world and are fighting the battle on earth and have not been called home to heaven constitute the CHURCH MILITANT.

subject: DOC
topic: The Apostle's Creed and its Explanation
front: What does "catholic" mean?
back: It is probably derived from the Greek adverbial phrase kath' holou, "on the whole". The Catholic Church means the Universal Church - all people throughout the world who believe in Jesus Christ as Saviour and Lord.
excerpt: The word catholic is probably derived from the Greek adverbial phrase kath' holou, which means on the whole.

subject: DOC
front: What is the millennium, and why do Christians disagree about it?
back: A period of one thousand years during which Jesus is to reign upon earth. Some see this as a specific future period, some as symbolic of the age of the church in which we are now living; and even those who take it as a future period differ as to where it fits with other events.
excerpt: They disagree about the millennium, a period of one thousand years during which Jesus is to reign upon earth

subject: DOC
front: How prominent is the return of Christ in the New Testament?
back: One verse in twenty-five deals with the Lord's return; the subject is mentioned 318 times in the 260 chapters, and appears in every New Testament book except Galatians and the very short books such as 2 and 3 John and Philemon.
excerpt: In the New Testament, one verse in twenty-five deals with the Lord's return. The subject is mentioned 318 times in the 260 chapters.

subject: DOC
front: What did Paul and Peter call the return of Christ?
back: Paul called it "our blessed hope" (Titus 2:13); Peter called it our "living hope" (1 Pet. 1:3).
excerpt: Paul called the return of Jesus Christ "our blessed hope" (Titus 2:13).

subject: DOC
front: How does God save us in spirit, soul and body?
back: He gives us a new spirit in the moment of the new birth; he creates a new soul through the process of sanctification; and at the resurrection he gives us a new body. The salvation he provides is a complete salvation.
excerpt: He gives us a new spirit in the moment of the new birth. He creates a new soul through the process of sanctification. At the resurrection he gives us a new body.

subject: DOC
front: Which three parables did Jesus use to teach what the final judgment would be like?
back: The Parable of the Ten Virgins (Maidens) - Matthew 25:1-13; the Parable of the Talents - Matthew 25:14-30; and the Parable of the Sheep and Goats - Matthew 25:31-46.
excerpt: The Parable of the Ten Virgins (Maidens) 	-     Matthew 25:1-13

subject: DOC
front: What four features do all three judgment parables share?
back: There is a sudden return of the Lord; some are prepared for his coming and others are not; there are rewards and judgments; and those who are lost are no doubt amazed at that outcome.
excerpt: All three parables contain the same essential features, though each is different from the others in detail.

subject: LIT
front: What are the "sentences" in the liturgy?
back: Scriptural passages selected to be read to the congregation at worship services; those in the liturgy are for guidance and others may be selected to suit specific occasions.
excerpt: These are scriptural passages selected to be read to the congregation at worship services.

subject: LIT
front: Name the four "preliminaries" which preceded the readings from the late seventh century.
back: The Introit, the Kyries, the Gloria and the Collect.
excerpt: the readings were preceded by four distinct items: The Introit, The Kyries, The Gloria, and Collect. These are known as the preliminaries.

subject: LIT
front: From what word does "Introit" come, and what does it mean?
back: From the Latin "introitus", meaning entry or entrance. It is a hymn or psalm sung when the ministers enter at the opening of a service.
excerpt: comes from a Latin word "introitus" which means entry or entrance.

subject: LIT
front: To what date and to which Pope do older liturgists trace the Introit?
back: To the fifth century, and to Pope Celestine 1 (d. 432).
excerpt: The introit, according to older liturgists, dates from the fifth century, from Pope Celestine 1 (d. 432).

subject: LIT
front: What does "Kyrie eleison" mean, and what does it stand for?
back: It stands for Invocation in the Greek language and means "Lord have mercy."
excerpt: Background: This stands for Invocation in the Greek language, "Lord have mercy."

subject: LIT
front: What is the Gloria, and where does its opening line come from?
back: An ancient hymn of praise to the Trinity, in use since the second century; its opening line is taken from Luke 2:14, where the angels announce the birth of Christ to the shepherds.
excerpt: The Gloria is an ancient hymn of praise to the Trinity that has been in use in the Church since the second century.

subject: LIT
front: From what does the name "Collect" derive?
back: From the Gallican rite, Collectio, later Collecta; it refers to the collecting or summing up of the people's intercession, and comes from the Latin meaning to bring together into a sentence.
excerpt: The name derives from the Gallican rite, Collectio, later Collecta; and refers to the function of the prayer, to its collecting or summing up of the people's intercession, as was once thought.

subject: LIT
front: What are the five parts of the form of a Collect?
back: An address to God; a clause referring to some attribute or saving act of God; the petition; the purpose for which we ask; the conclusion.
excerpt: Their form consists of:

subject: LIT
front: Which canticles are chanted between the readings in modern Ghanaian Methodist worship?
back: The Te Deum Laudamus, Venite Exultemus Domino, Benedicite Omnia Opera and the Cantemus Cuncti.
excerpt: canticles like the Te Deum Laudamus, Venite Exultemus Domino, Benedicite Omnia Opera and the Cantemus Cuncti are chanted in between the readings.

subject: LIT
front: Which creeds are commonly used among Ghanaian Methodists?
back: The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed. Creeds confirm the faithful in their faith and strengthen their corporate unity.
excerpt: The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed are the commonly used among Ghanaian Methodists in affirming our faith.

subject: LIT
topic: Outline Of The New Order For Sunday Morning Worship
front: What are the first five items of the New Order for Sunday Morning Worship?
back: Call to Worship; Introit; Hymn; Prayer; Hymn/Lyric.
excerpt: Call to Worship

subject: LIT
topic: Outline Of The New Order For Sunday Morning Worship
front: What four items make up the Ministry of the Word in the New Order?
back: The Old Testament, the Epistle, the Te Deum and the Gospel Reading.
excerpt: The Ministry of the Word

subject: LIT
topic: Outline Of The New Order For Sunday Morning Worship
front: What are the last five items of the New Order for Sunday Morning Worship?
back: Invitation to Christian Discipleship; Announcements; Tithes and Offertory; Hymn; Benediction and Dismissal.
excerpt: Benediction and Dismissal

subject: LIT
front: When is the Apostles' Creed used, and when the Nicene Creed?
back: The Apostles' Creed on ordinary occasions; the Nicene Creed on Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days.
excerpt:
Generally, the Apostle's Creed is said on ordinary occasions and the Nicene Creed on 
Communion Sundays, Christmas, Easter and other special days.

subject: LIT
front: What is the purpose of a creed, and what did the Greek "sumbolon" mean?
back: A creed acts as a yardstick of correct belief. Sumbolon meant half of a broken object which, placed with the other half, verified the bearer's identity.
excerpt: The purpose of a creed is to act as a yardstick of correct belief.

subject: LIT
front: Where and when was the Nicene Creed adopted, and against whom?
back: In the city of Nicaea in 325, in the face of the Arian controversy raised by Arius, a Libyan preacher.
excerpt: It is called Nicene because, in its original form, it was adopted in the city of Nicaea in 325.

subject: LIT
front: How does Bernard Manning describe preaching the sermon?
back: As a "manifestation of the Incarnate Word, from the written word, by the spoken word"; also as an assault upon Hell's gate and a deed not of man but of God.
excerpt:
Bernard Manning therefore sees preaching the sermon as "manifestation of the Incarnate 
Word, from the written word, by the spoken word".

subject: LIT
front: How does Bultman define preaching?
back: As "the communication of Biblical truth by man to man with the explicit purpose of eliciting behavourial change".
excerpt: Bultman also defines preaching as "the communication of Biblical truth by man to man with the explicit purpose of eliciting behavourial change".

subject: LIT
front: What are the three purposes of preaching?
back: Proclaiming the Gospel (kerygmatic), teaching (didactic), and therapeutic — aimed at healing the broken spirit and broken society.
excerpt: The purposes of preaching then are: proclaiming the Gospel (kerygmatic), teaching (didactic) as well as it being therapeutic i.e. aimed at healing the broken spirit and broken society.

subject: LIT
front: From what does the word "text" come, and what does it imply?
back: From the Latin "textus"; it implies something woven. In a topical sermon there may be no need to choose a text.
excerpt: The word text is from the Latin 'textus'. It implies something woven.

subject: LIT
front: How are exegesis and hermeneutics distinguished?
back: Exegesis aims at understanding the text in itself; hermeneutics attempts to elucidate what the text means for the modern interpreter and the people of his culture.
excerpt: "Exegesis aims at understanding the text in itself while hermeneutics attempts to elucidate what the text means for the modern interpreter and the people of his culture."

subject: LIT
front: What are the steps in exegesis?
back: The text; the context; the historical setting; the geography of the land of the Bible; culture; and the circumstances peculiar to the writer.
excerpt:
The following points help the preacher in his/her sermon preparation to undertake a 
proper exegesis:

subject: LIT
front: How have sermons been described in the syllabus?
back: As personal testimony, biographical, historical incident, topical, textual, expository, springboard or narrative.
excerpt: Sermons have been described as personal testimony, biographical, historical incident, topical, textual, expository, springboard or narrative.

subject: LIT
front: What is a topical sermon?
back: Preaching on a subject: one chooses the subject, finds all the Scripture relating to it and forms that material into a sermon. It takes only its subject from the text.
excerpt: A Topical Sermon is preaching on a subject. One chooses the subject and then finds all the Scripture that relates to that subject and forms that material into a sermon.

subject: LIT
front: What is a textual sermon, and what method does it use?
back: The preacher takes a few verses, a verse or part of a verse, discovers its theme in context and preaches on it in his own words, using the "hook-book-look-and took" method.
excerpt:
In Textual sermons, the preacher takes a few verses, a verse, or even a part of a verse from 
the Bible.

subject: LIT
front: What is an expository sermon?
back: The preacher selects a paragraph of Scripture, discovers the theme from the passage and develops it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs.
excerpt: Preachers who preach expository sermons select a paragraph of Scripture, discover the theme from the passage and develop it point by point using evidence from the chosen paragraphs.

subject: LIT
front: What three elements aid the study of a passage for an expository sermon?
back: Statements (sentences that report facts); Expressions (which demonstrate emotion); Prescriptive (sentences that describe what is to be done).
excerpt: 1. Statements: These elements are sentences that report facts.

subject: LIT
front: What is eisegesis?
back: The "art" of reading preconceived opinions into the text, as opposed to exegesis, the honest critical analysis or interpretation of the passage.
excerpt:
Eisegesis (the "art" of reading preconceived 
opinions into the text)

subject: LIT
front: What is "the peak of your delivery"?
back: The point in the sermon where anything said again brings down the excitement and joy of the listeners.
excerpt: The peak of your delivery is the point in your sermon where, anything said again brings down the excitement and the joy of your listeners.

subject: LIT
front: When is the most appropriate time to select hymns?
back: When you have finished preparing your sermon, or at least when the first draft, outline or sketch is done.
excerpt:
The most appropriate time to select your hymns is when you have finished preparing your sermon or at least when the first draft, 
outline or sketch, as you may call it, is done.

subject: LIT
front: What are the roles of the four hymns in a Methodist service?
back: First: praise and/or adoration. Second: invocation. Third: the sermon hymn. Closing: the hymn of response.
excerpt: The first hymn in our services always serves as hymn of praise and/or adoration.

subject: LIT
front: Which MHB ranges are named for the hymn of praise and the hymn of invocation?
back: Praise: MHB 1 to 35 and MHB 82 to 116. Invocation: MHB 273 to MHB 301.
excerpt:
Preachers have often 
chosen hymns from MHB 273 to MHB 301 as the second hymn.

subject: LIT
topic: Factors to Consider in Choosing the Sermon Hymn and the Closing Hymn
front: What is "the proposition" in a sermon?
back: The central thought in the sermon; it contains the main message and the desired response, and is thought to do the best job as an aid to hymn selection.
excerpt: The proposition is the central thought in the sermon. It contains the main message and the desired response.

subject: LIT
front: What is the major problem preachers face which makes hymn selection suffer?
back: The time to get settled and prepare sermons; many prepare on Saturday night or Sunday morning.
excerpt: One major problem preachers commonly face is the time to get settled and prepare sermons.

subject: LIT
front: What is prayer?
back: A conversation or communication with God; the means by which we link our souls with the Spirit of God and convey our heart's desires and concerns to Him.
excerpt: Prayer is a conversation or communication with God.

subject: LIT
front: What did John Wesley say about prayer in his sermon "Means of Grace"?
back: "All who desire the grace of God are to wait for it in the way of prayer."
excerpt: John Wesley, in his sermon, "Means of Grace," said, "All who desire the grace of God are to wait for it in the way of prayer."

subject: LIT
front: What does P.U.S.H. mean?
back: "Pray Until Something Happens" — after asking without receiving and seeking without finding, you must knock hard.
excerpt: you may need to P.U.S.H. -literally meaning 'Pray Until Something Happens.'

subject: LIT
front: Who was George Muller, and what does his example teach?
back: A German-born English preacher, a man of prayer who lived by faith. He prayed for five people; the last was saved after fifty-two years, just after Muller's death.
excerpt: George Muller was a German-born English preacher and was referred to as a man of prayer who lived by faith.

subject: LIT
front: What are the four elements of the content of prayer?
back: CATS (Confession, Adoration, Thanksgiving and Supplication) or ACTS (Adoration, Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication).
excerpt:
This formula is popularly known as CATS (Confession, Adoration, Thanksgiving and Supplication) or ACTS (Adoration, 
Confession, Thanksgiving and Supplication).

subject: LIT
front: What does supplication include?
back: Petition, which is asking God for personal things, and intercession, which is prayer for others.
excerpt: Supplication includes petition for our own needs and intercession for others.

subject: LIT
front: What attitudes does prayer generate?
back: Trust, faith, confidence and hope; also humility, self-abasement and self-surrender.
excerpt: There is intimacy which generates the attitude of trust, faith, confidence and hope. Other attitudes are humility, self-abasement, and self-surrender.

subject: LIT
front: Name the general Christian festivals in the order in which they appear on the calendar.
back: Advent Sunday, Christmas, Epiphany, Ash Wednesday, Lent, Palm Sunday, Good Friday, Easter (Resurrection Day), Ascension, Pentecost, Trinity.
excerpt:
The general ones are listed below in the order of appearance on the 
Christian calendar and the time of year celebrated.

subject: LIT
topic: Background to the Date for Easter Celebration
front: Who were the "Quartodecimans"?
back: Those who kept Easter on the 14th Nisan, the same day as the Jewish Passover, whatever the day of the week.
excerpt: Those who kept Easter on the 14th Nisan were known as "Quartodecimans".

subject: LIT
front: When is Pentecost celebrated, and what was it in Judaism?
back: On the 50th day after Easter, the 7th Sunday after Easter. In Judaism it was a harvest festival, also known as the Feast of Weeks and the Feast of First Fruits.
excerpt:
In Judaism, Pentecost was a harvest festival which was also known as the Feast of Weeks 
(Lev. 23:5-21), the Feast of First Fruits.

subject: LIT
front: Why is Pentecost called Whitsunday, and what did Athanasius call it?
back: From the white robes worn by catechumens baptized that day, or from "wit" meaning wisdom. Athanasius called it "Magna Dominica", the "Great Sunday".
excerpt: St. Athanasius calls it "Magna Dominica" the "Great Sunday"

subject: LIT
front: What is Lent, and where does the word come from?
back: A period of 40 days, determined by the length of our Lord's fast in the wilderness. The word comes from the Anglo Saxon "Lenten", meaning "spring". It runs from Ash Wednesday to Holy Saturday.
excerpt: The word lent comes from an Anglo Saxon word "Lenten" which means "spring".

subject: LIT
front: What does "Epiphany" mean, and what was it connected with?
back: From the Greek epiphania, meaning manifestation; it also stands for "appearing". It was connected with Christ's baptism, nativity and the miracle at Cana.
excerpt: Epiphany comes from, the Greek word epiphania, which means manifestation.

subject: LIT
front: From what is the word "Christmas" derived?
back: From Christ + Mass: the special mass or worship service said during the celebration of Christ's birth, from the season's first service, the Christ Mass.
excerpt: The word Christmas is derived from a combination of two words i.e. Christ + Mass.

subject: LIT
front: What are the four Sundays of Advent about?
back: The second coming of Christ (Advent Sunday); preparation for the incarnation in Old Testament prophecy; the ministry of John the Baptist; and the vocations of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St. Joseph.
excerpt:
These are the second coming of Christ (Advent Sunday), 
Preparation for the incarnation in Old Testament prophecy, the Ministry of John the 
Baptist, and the vocations of Blessed Virgin Mary and St. Joseph.

subject: LIT
front: When and where was the first Covenant Service held?
back: In the French Church at Spitfalfields on August 11, 1755, when Wesley recited the words of Richard Alleine. Covenant Sunday is peculiar to Methodists all over the world.
excerpt: His first Covenant Service was held in the French Church at Spitfalfields on August 11, 1755, when he recited the words of "that blessed man Richard Alleine"

subject: LIT
front: What are the two cycles of the Christian year, and their sequence of colours?
back: The Christmas Cycle (Advent-Christmas-Epiphany) and the Easter Cycle (Lent-Easter-Pentecost). In each: purple for the preparatory season, white for the festival season, green for ordinary time.
excerpt: The Christian year contains two cycles: The Christmas Cycle (Advent-Christmas-Epiphany) and the Easter Cycle (Lent-Easter-Pentecost).

subject: LIT
front: What does purple signify, and when is it used?
back: Both penitence and royalty; used during the preparatory seasons of Advent and Lent. Blue, a colour of hope, may also be used during Advent.
excerpt:
Purple is a colour of both penitence and royalty used during the preparatory seasons of 
Advent and Lent.

subject: LIT
front: When are white and gold used?
back: During the Christmas and Easter seasons (except on the Day of Pentecost), on festive days such as Baptism of the Lord, Transfiguration, Trinity, All Saints and Christ the King, and at weddings, baptisms and Holy Communion.
excerpt:
White and gold are joyous and festive colours used during the Christmas and Easter 
Seasons (except on the Day of Pentecost)

subject: LIT
front: What does red signify, and when is it used?
back: It is the colour of fire, symbolizing the Holy Spirit, and also the blood of Christ and of the martyrs. It is used on the Day of Pentecost, for evangelistic services, ordinations, consecrations, anniversaries and homecomings, and in Holy Week from Passion/Palm Sunday.
excerpt: Red is a colour of fire, symbolizing the Hoy Spirit.

subject: LIT
front: What does green signify, and when is it used?
back: It is a colour of growth, used in the seasons after Epiphany and after Pentecost, except when special days call for white or red.
excerpt: Green is a colour of growth, used in the seasons after Epiphany and after Pentecost except when special days call for white or red.

subject: LIT
front: What is culture?
back: The accumulated habits, attitudes and beliefs of a group of people that define for them their general behaviour and way of life. It is dynamic, progressive, interactive, "maturational" and "acquisitional".
excerpt: Culture may be viewed as the accumulated habits, attitudes, and beliefs of a group of people that define for them their general behavior and way of life.

subject: LIT
topic: THE MEANING OF CULTURAL RELEVANCE OF WORSHIP
front: What is the cultural relevance of worship?
back: A process by which the church, in its mission of preaching the gospel, becomes culturally sensitive and thus relevant to her context while remaining doctrinally pure. It is not political correctness nor a watering down of the gospel.
excerpt: Rather it is a process by which the church, in its mission of preaching the gospel, becomes culturally sensitive and thus relevant to her context while remaining doctrinally pure.

subject: LIT
front: What are the three "unchangeables" in worship?
back: Jesus; the Word of God; and Divine Principles.
excerpt: 4.1.1	 Jesus

subject: LIT
front: What are the "changeables" in worship?
back: Change comes with age; ministry methods change (worship styles, technology, outreach and teaching methods); and God Himself is a God of change.
excerpt: We change physically as we age.

subject: LIT
front: What is a worldview, and what three things help the church meet the challenge of cultural relevance?
back: A worldview is the lenses through which we see our world. The three are: obtain a biblical worldview; embrace new methodologies; be creative in worship.
excerpt: A worldview is quite simply the lenses through which we see our world.

subject: MS
front: What are the four sources of Wesley's theological thinking?
back: Scripture, Reason, Tradition and Experience — the Wesleyan Quadrilateral.
excerpt: The Source of Wesley's theological thinking is four-fold; namely Scripture, Reason, Tradition and Experience. This is normally referred to as the Wesleyan Quadrilateral.

subject: MS
front: What did the deed of every Methodist preaching house provide about doctrine?
back: That if a preacher's doctrine or practice was, in the opinion of the major part of the trustees, not conformable to Mr Wesley's Sermons and Notes on the New Testament, another preacher should be sent within three months.
excerpt: In case the doctrine or practice of any preacher should, in the opinion of the major part of the trustees, be not conformable to Mr. Wesley's Sermons and Notes on the New Testament, on representing this another preacher shall be sent within three months.

subject: MS
front: What did Wesley mean by calling himself Homo Unius Libri?
back: A man of one Book. In his Journal for May 14, 1765 he wrote, “In 1730 I began to be Homo Unius Libri, to study comparatively no book but the Bible.”
excerpt: John Wesley called himself Homo Unius Libri - A man of one Book.

subject: MS
front: How did Wesley describe reason?
back: As “this Precious gift of God”; he also said, “I am ready to give up every opinion which I cannot by calm, clear reason defend.”
excerpt: He referred to reason as "this Precious gift of God"

subject: MS
front: What did Wesley say in “A Short History of Methodism” about the Methodists and the Bible?
back: “It is the Methodists' one desire and design to be downright Bible Christians; taking the Bible, as interpreted by the primitive Church and our own, for their whole and sole rule.” — “our own” means the Church of England.
excerpt: "It is the Methodists' one desire and design to be downright Bible Christians; taking the Bible, as interpreted by the primitive Church and our own, for their whole and sole rule."

subject: MS
front: Under what three main themes can Wesley's understanding of human nature be classified?
back: (a) Humanity as God's gracious creation, (b) humanity as fallen, and (c) humanity as freshly restored.
excerpt: Wesley's understanding of human nature can be classified under three main themes: (a) Humanity as God's gracious creation (b) Humanity as fallen and (c) Humanity as freshly restored.

subject: MS
front: Of what four elements did Wesley say the human body is composed?
back: Dust, water, air and fire, all duly proportioned and mixed together; the body is “a little portion of earth”.
excerpt: Wesley claimed that the human body is composed of four elements, namely, dust, water, air and fire all duly proportioned and mixed together.

subject: MS
front: Under which three images did Wesley discuss man created in the image of God?
back: The natural, the political and the moral images of God.
excerpt: Wesley discussed man created in the image of God under three images: the natural, political and moral images of God.

subject: MS
front: Which scripture guided Wesley's account of the moral image, and why was it the principal image?
back: Ephesians 4:24. Man was made holy as God is holy, merciful, perfect, pure and inwardly and outwardly sinless; for Wesley the moral image was the principal image.
excerpt: Using Ephesians 4:24 as his guide, Wesley stressed that man was made in the image of God; holy as God who created him is holy, merciful as the author of all is merciful, perfect as his Father in heaven is perfect.

subject: MS
front: According to Wesley, what caused Adam's fall, and what caused Lucifer's?
back: Adam fell first as a result of unbelief, a lack of trust in God; Lucifer was self-tempted and gave way first to pride, then to self-will.
excerpt: Wesley maintained that Adam fell, first as a result of unbelief, a lack of trust in God.

subject: MS
front: Into whose images did Adam sink when he lost the moral image of God?
back: Partly into the image of the Devil, in pride, malice and other evil dispositions, and partly into the image of the brute, under brutal passions and degrading appetites.
excerpt: Adam sunk partly into the image of the Devil, in pride, malice and in other evil dispositions and partly into the image of the brute, having fallen under the power of brutal passions and degrading appetites.

subject: MS
front: Whose writings gave rise to the doctrine of original sin, and which passages did Wesley cite for it?
back: The writings of Saint Augustine. Wesley cited Genesis 3:1ff, Psalm 5:5 and Romans 5:12-21.
excerpt: The doctrine of original sin came about as the church reflected on the writings of Saint  Augustine as to how the fall of Adam and Eve affected the rest of humanity.

subject: MS
front: What fourfold inheritance did Adam and Eve bequeath to humanity, according to Wesley?
back: Unbelief, pride, self-will and love of the world — the last with three components: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eye and the pride of life.
excerpt: Thus unbelief, pride, self-will and love of the world are the inheritance that Adam and Eve bequeathed to humanity.

subject: MS
front: Define prevenient grace.
back: The grace which goes before any human action for salvation; it acts before any individual has any thought of turning to the Christian faith. It may also be called antecedent grace: God seeks us before we ever seek God.
excerpt: Wesley used the term prevenient grace to mean that grace which goes before any human action for salvation.

subject: MS
front: What did Wesley mean by saying grace is “free in all”?
back: “The grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is free in all. It is free in all to whom it is given. It does not depend on any power or merit in man; no, not in any degree, neither in whole, nor in part.”
excerpt: The grace or love of God, whence cometh our salvation, is free in all. It is free in all to whom it is given. It does not depend on any power or merit in man; no, not in any degree, neither in whole, nor in part.

subject: MS
front: What does Wesley call repentance, and what leads to it?
back: Repentance is “the porch of religion”; prevenient grace stirs us to repentance, and repentance or conviction of sin always precedes faith.
excerpt: Prevenient grace only serves to stir us to repentance, which Wesley calls the porch of religion.

subject: MS
front: State three things that justification is NOT, according to Wesley.
back: It is not doing things that are just and righteous; it is not God clearing us from the accusations of Satan; and it is not the clearing of us from the accusation brought against us by the law.
excerpt: Also, justification is not God clearing us from the accusations of Satan. In addition, justification is not the clearing us from the accusation brought against us by the law.

subject: MS
front: What is justification according to Wesley?
back: Pardon, the forgiveness of sins — the act of God the Father whereby, for the sake of the propitiation made by the blood of his Son, he showed forth his righteousness by the remission of the sins that are past.
excerpt:
What then is justification? According to Wesley, justification is pardon, the forgiveness of 
sins. It is the act of God the Father, whereby, for the sake of the propitiation (sacrifice) made by the blood of his Son, he showed forth his righteousness by the remission (forgiveness) of the sins that are past.

subject: MS
front: Whom does God justify?
back: The ungodly of every kind and every degree. It is not a saint but a sinner that is forgiven; no sinner is too sinful to be disqualified from God's forgiveness.
excerpt: Wesley pointed out that God justified the ungodly of every kind and every degree.

subject: MS
front: What are the results of justification?
back: Joy in our faith (the faith of a son rather than the faith of a servant), the freedom to live as a free person — not perfect but accepted and forgiven — and love, works, generosity, personal and social holiness.
excerpt: Other results of justification are love, works, and generosity, personal and social holiness.

subject: MS
front: How did Wesley distinguish justification from sanctification?
back: “By justification we are saved from the guilt of sin and restored to the favour of God. By sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God.”
excerpt: "By justification we are saved from the guilt of sin and restored to the favour of God. By sanctification we are saved from the power and root of sin and restored to the image of God.

subject: MS
front: What did Wesley call the inner work of the Holy Spirit that produces holy living?
back: Christian Perfection. Sanctification is the process of growth into the image of God and begins the moment a person is justified.
excerpt: It is this holy living which Wesley called Christian Perfection.

subject: MS
front: How does Wesley define Christian perfection, and what other names does he give it?
back: Pure love in the heart and life of man — loving God and loving our neighbour. He also called it the Second Blessing, Entire Sanctification, Full Sanctification and Full Salvation.
excerpt: John Wesley defines Christian perfection as pure love in the heart and life of man.

subject: MS
front: What did Wesley say in 1790 about Christian perfection and the Methodists?
back: That Christian perfection is “the grand deposit” which God has lodged with the people called Methodists, and that He appeared to have raised them up mainly to propagate that message.
excerpt: In 1790, a year before he died, he stressed that Christian perfection is the grand deposit, which God has lodged with the people called Methodists

subject: MS
front: What was George Whitefield's objection to Wesley's teaching on Christian perfection?
back: He claimed that there is no such perfection on earth.
excerpt: Wesley's teaching on Christian perfection was opposed by people like George Whitefield who claimed that there is no such perfection on earth.

subject: MS
topic: What Christian Perfection is NOT according to John Wesley
front: In which treatise and year did Wesley publish his understanding of Christian perfection, and who had misunderstood it?
back: “A Plain Account of Christian Perfection”, published in 1766. His critics included the Moravians and the Calvinists.
excerpt: Wesley published his understanding of this doctrine in 1766 in his treatise entitled, "A plain Account of Christian Perfection."

subject: MS
topic: What Christian Perfection is NOT according to John Wesley
front: In what senses did Wesley say Christians are NOT perfect?
back: They are not perfect in knowledge, not free from ignorance or mistake, not free from infirmities, and not wholly free from temptation — for the servant is not above his Master.
excerpt: Christians are not perfect in knowledge. They are not free from ignorance; or from mistake.

subject: MS
front: When did Wesley believe entire sanctification is normally received?
back: It is instantaneous but preceded and followed by gradual work, and this gift of grace is not usually received until just prior to death.
excerpt: Wesley stressed that entire sanctification is instantaneous but it is preceded by and followed by gradual work.

subject: MS
front: When and where was Charles Wesley born?
back: At Epworth on 18th December 1707; he was the youngest of the three male children to survive to adulthood.
excerpt: Charles Wesley was born in Epworth on 18th December 1707.

subject: MS
front: What was the Holy Club, and what nickname did it earn Charles Wesley?
back: A devotional group of like-minded students he gathered at Oxford to study Scripture and partake of the Sacrament. It gained him “the harmless nickname of Methodist”.
excerpt: It was called the Holy Club.

subject: MS
front: When was Charles Wesley converted, and what had he been reading?
back: On 21st May 1738, after reading through Luther's commentary on the Book of Galatians — three days before his brother John.
excerpt: Charles Wesley had his spiritual conversion on 21st May 1738 after reading through Luther's commentary on the Book of Galatians.

subject: MS
front: Whose saying lies behind “O for a thousand tongues to sing” (MHB 1)?
back: Peter Bohler's: “Had I a thousand tongues, I would praise Him with them all.” Charles turned it into a hymn to mark the anniversary of his conversion.
excerpt: Peter Bohler is said to have told Charles, "Had I a thousand tongues, I would praise Him with them all."

subject: MS
topic: The Use of the Bible in the Methodist Hymns
front: What did John Wesley write about the Bible in 1729, and what is the effect on the hymns?
back: “I began not only to read but to study the Bible.” The hymns are in many cases a mere mosaic of biblical passages or extracts.
excerpt: In the year 1729, John Wesley wrote, "I began not only to read but to study the Bible."

subject: MS
topic: The Use of the Bible in the Methodist Hymns
front: What did Charles Wesley publish in 1762?
back: A collection of Short Hymns on Select Passages of the Holy Scriptures, a kind of devotional commentary in verse.
excerpt: In 1762 Charles published a collection of Short Hymns on Select Passages of the Holy Scriptures, a kind of devotional commentary in verse.

subject: MS
topic: The Use of the Bible in the Methodist Hymns
front: On what passage is “Wrestling Jacob” (MHB 339) based, and who praised it?
back: Genesis 32:21-32. Isaac Watts declared that this single poem was worth all the verses he himself had written.
excerpt: Another, generally thought to be his greatest hymn, is based on Genesis 32:21-32.

subject: MS
topic: The Hymns and the Great Festivals of the Church
front: Name Charles Wesley's hymns for the great festivals of the Church.
back: Christmas: “Hark, the herald angel sing”; Easter: “Christ the Lord is risen today”; Ascensiontide: “Hail the day that sees him rise” (MHB 221); Whit Sunday: “Away with our fears” (MHB 278).
excerpt:
There are few 
churches of any denomination which do not celebrate Christmas with "Hark, the herald 
angel sing" or Easter with "Christ the Lord is risen today".

subject: MS
topic: The Sacraments in the Methodist Hymns
front: On whose article were Charles Wesley's Hymns on the Lord's Supper based?
back: An article by a high church divine, Dr. Daniel Brevint; they expressed the Wesleys' high doctrine of the Sacrament as a celebration of Christ's sacrificial love for mankind.
excerpt: Charles Wesley's Hymns on the Lord's Supper, based on an article by a high church divine, Dr. Daniel Brevint, expressed the Wesley's high doctrine of the Sacrament as a celebration of Christ's sacrificial love for mankind.

subject: MS
topic: The Sacraments in the Methodist Hymns
front: What did the Wesleys mean, and not mean, by Christ's “real presence” in the Sacrament?
back: “Real” did not mean “physical”, nor that the bread and wine were changed. Any change was in the relationship between the worshipper and God; the sacrament was a “means of grace”.
excerpt:
It must be noted however, that the "real" did not mean "physical" or imply that the 
elements of bread and wine were changed in some way.

subject: MS
front: How did John Wesley sum up the difference between himself and Charles?
back: “In connexion I beat you; but in strong, pointed sentences you beat me.”
excerpt:
"In 
connexion I beat you; but in strong, pointed sentences you beat me".

subject: MS
front: Whom did Charles Wesley marry, and when?
back: Sally Gwynne, whom he first met in Wales in August 1747; John Wesley married them in August 1748. In 1754 she was permanently disfigured by small pox.
excerpt: He first met Sally Gwynne during a visit to Wales in August 1747. She was nearly 21, about 19 years younger than him. John Wesley married them in August 1748.

subject: MS
front: When did Charles Wesley die?
back: He died peacefully in his home on 29th March 1788 and was buried on 5th April; as one of his preachers put it, he had no disorder but old age.
excerpt: He died peacefully in his home on 29th March 1788 and buried on 5th April.

subject: MS
front: What did Wesley say about Christianity and social religion?
back: “The Gospel of Christ knows no religion but social, no holiness but social holiness.” Christianity is essentially a social religion, and to turn it into a solitary religion is to destroy it.
excerpt: "The Gospel of Christ knows no religion but social, no holiness but social holiness".

subject: MS
front: What loan fund did Wesley establish for the poor?
back: From his own savings he provided the capital for interest-free loans of up to three months, first limited to twenty shillings and later raised to five pounds; within one year more than 250 persons had been helped.
excerpt:
From his own savings Wesley provided the basic capital of a loan fund from which the poor 
could take interest-free loans up to three months.

subject: MS
topic: John Wesley and the Use of Money
front: What are Wesley's three rules on the use of money?
back: “Gain all you can, Save all you can and Give all you can.” Those who observe the first two and not the third are twofold more the children of hell than ever they were before.
excerpt: These were: "Gain all you can, Save all you can and Give all you can".

subject: MS
front: Who started the Trans-Atlantic slave trade, and when did England join it?
back: The Portuguese started it; England joined in the latter part of 1550 and became the leading exporter of slaves from Africa to the American market.
excerpt:
The Trans-Atlantic slave trade was started by the Portuguese and England joined the trade 
in the latter part of 1550

subject: MS
front: Which cruelties of the slave trade did Wesley write about in 1774?
back: The cruelties of capturing, transporting and selling slaves, as well as the inhuman treatment by their owners, which reduced them to a status hardly preferable to beasts of burden.
excerpt:
Wesley wrote on the cruelties of capturing, transporting and selling slaves, as well as the 
inhuman treatment by their owners

subject: MS
front: Which anti-slavery leaders did Wesley support?
back: Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson and William Wilberforce. Wesley and Wilberforce met for the first time on 24 February 1789.
excerpt:
Wesley supported other anti-slavery leaders like Granville Sharp, Thomas Clarkson and 
William Wilberforce in their campaign against the slave trade.

subject: MS
front: What did the General Rule of Methodists say about liquor?
back: It forbade drunkenness, and the buying or selling of spirituous liquor or the drinking of them. Wesley opposed the liquor trade on social, humanitarian and religious grounds.
excerpt:
The General Rule of Methodists forbade drunkenness, buying or selling spirituous 
liquor or drinking them.

subject: MS
front: Who challenged Calvin's teaching on predestination, and who was commissioned to answer him?
back: Koornheert, a layman from Holland, challenged it in 1589; the church commissioned a young priest, Jacobus Arminius (1560-1609), to answer his charges.
excerpt:
This doctrine was challenged by Koornheert, a layman from Holland in 1589. The church 
commissioned a young priest Jacobus Arminius (1560-1609) to answer the charges of 
Koornheert.

subject: MS
front: What was the crux of the argument between the Calvinists and the Arminians?
back: Whether atonement was limited or universal. Arminianism argued that it is the will of God to save all persons.
excerpt: The crux of the argument was whether atonement was limited or universal.

subject: MS
front: What did Wesley deny in his 1740 sermon “Free Grace”?
back: The Calvinist view and all associated with it — “irresistible grace, limited atonement, perseverance of the saints and unconditional election”. He later told Whitefield, “your God is my devil.”
excerpt: He denied the Calvinist view and all that was associated with it - "irresistible grace, limited atonement, perseverance of the saints and unconditional election".

subject: MS
front: How did the Calvinist controversy divide the English Revival?
back: George Whitefield led the Calvinist Methodist connexion under the patronage of Lady Huntingdon, and Wesley's preachers John Cennick and John Humphrey joined the Calvinists; the conflict became the “Pamphlets of War”.
excerpt: The conflict brought a division in the English Revival with George Whitefield leading the Calvinist Methodists connexion under the patronage of Lady Huntingdon.

subject: MS
topic: Wesley and the Church of England (Anglican)
front: Whom did Wesley ordain in September 1784 for America, and why?
back: Dr. Thomas Coke as superintendent, with Richard Whatcoat and Thomas Vasey as Elders, after Bishop Lowth of London refused his request of August 1780 to ordain preachers for America.
excerpt:
Therefore in September 1784 Wesley 
ordained Dr. Thomas Coke as superintendent and Richard Whatcoat and Thomas Vasey as 
Elders for America.

subject: MS
front: Which District Synod began the move towards Episcopal Leadership in Ghana Methodism, and in what year?
back: The Kumasi District Synod, in 1990; its Chairman, Rt. Rev'd Samuel Asante Antwi, submitted a proposal to the Conference meeting at Koforidua that same year.
excerpt:
In 
1990 the Kumasi District Synod started the discussions that would move the Methodist 
Church Ghana towards Episcopal Leadership.

subject: MS
front: Which district first implemented the idea of a separated Chairman as a move towards the Episcopal system?
back: The Kumasi District, in 1992; Kumasi was followed by the Sunyani District. Only Kumasi and Sunyani had been fully in favour of the system.
excerpt:
In 
1992 the Kumasi District implemented the idea of a separated Chairman as a move 
towards the Episcopal system. Kumasi was followed by the Sunyani District.

subject: MS
front: When and where was the Service of Proclamation held?
back: On Sunday, 23 January 2000 at 8.30am at the Wesley Methodist Church, Asafoatse Nettey Road, Accra.
excerpt:
A Service of Proclamation was held on Sunday, January 23, 2000 at the Wesley Methodist 
Church, Asafoatse Nettey Road, Accra at 8.30am.

subject: MS
front: What became of the President and Vice President of Conference under the Episcopal system?
back: The President of the Conference became the Presiding Bishop, referred to as “The Most Reverend...”; the Vice President became the Lay President of the Methodist Church Ghana.
excerpt:
The Presiding Bishop - The President of the Conference shall be known as the 
Presiding Bishop of the Methodist Church Ghana and referred to as "The Most  Reverend..."

subject: MS
front: What titles were given to Diocesan Bishops, Superintendent Ministers, Elders and Deacons?
back: Diocesan Bishops (formerly Chairmen and General Superintendents) — “The Right Reverend...”; Superintendent Ministers — “The Very Reverend...”; all ordained ministers are Elders — “The Reverend...”; all probationers or ministers-on-trial are Deacons — “The Reverend...”.
excerpt: Diocesan Bishops - The Chairman and General Superintendents of Districts shall be known as Diocesan Bishops and referred to as 'The Right Reverend. . ."

subject: NT
front: Who wrote the Gospel according to Mark, and what was his relationship to Paul and to Peter?
back: John Mark. He was not one of the Twelve, but he accompanied Paul on his missionary journey (Acts 13:13), and Peter called him his 'son' (1 Pet. 5:13). Papias and Irenaeus described him as Peter's interpreter.
excerpt: Author: John Mark. He was not one of the Twelve apostles but he accompanied Paul on his missionary journey (Acts 13: 13). The apostle Peter referred to Mark as his "son" (1 Pet. 5: 13).

subject: NT
front: When was the Gospel of Mark written, and in what setting?
back: Between A.D. 55 and 65, in the Roman Empire under Tiberius Caesar.
excerpt: Date Written: Between A. D. 55 and 65.

subject: NT
front: What is the key verse of Mark's Gospel?
back: 'For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many' (Mark 10:45).
excerpt: Key Verse: "For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life a ransom for many" (10: 45).

subject: NT
front: What three special features of Mark's Gospel does the syllabus name?
back: It was the first Gospel written; the other Gospels quote all except 31 verses of Mark; and it records more miracles than any other Gospel.
excerpt: Special Features: The Book was the first Gospel written. The other Gospels quote all except 31 verses of Mark. The Book of Mark records more miracles than does any other Gospel.

subject: NT
front: Which key places does the syllabus list for the Gospel of Mark?
back: Capernaum, Nazareth, Caesarea Philippi, Jericho, Bethany, the Mount of Olives, Jerusalem and Golgotha.
excerpt:
Key Places: Capernaum, Nazareth, Caesarea, Philippi, Jericho, Bethany, Mount of Olives, 
Jerusalem, Golgotha.

subject: NT
front: What is the meaning of the name 'Jesus', and of the title 'Christ'?
back: 'Jesus' is His divinely given personal name, whose Hebrew equivalent is 'Joshua', that is, 'Yaweh is Salvation'; 'Christ' is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew title Masiah (Messiah, Anointed).
excerpt: Its Hebrew equivalent (of the Greek is) "Joshua" i.e. "Yaweh" is Salvation. "Christ" is the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew title Masiah (Messiah, Anointed).

subject: NT
front: Which town became the hub of Jesus' Galilean ministry, and whose hometown was it?
back: Capernaum, the hometown of the four disciples who first accompanied Him.
excerpt: The four disciples accompanied Jesus into nearby Capernaum. It was their hometown and it became the hub of Jesus' Galilean ministry

subject: NT
front: On which three occasions does Mark portray Jesus at prayer?
back: Near the beginning of the account (1:35), near the middle (6:46) and near the end (14:32-42) - each in a setting of darkness and aloneness, when facing His messianic mission.
excerpt: Mark selectively portrayed Jesus at prayer on three crucial occasions, each in a setting of darkness and aloneness:

subject: NT
front: How did Jesus answer the criticism that His disciples did not fast?
back: His presence among His people was as much an occasion for rejoicing as a bridegroom among the wedding guests; but a time would come when the Bridegroom would be taken from them, and in that day - His crucifixion - the disciples would fast.
excerpt: Jesus' reply was that His presence among His people was as much an occasion for rejoicing as was that of a bridegroom among the guests at his wedding.

subject: NT
front: What two principles emerge from Jesus' reply about plucking grain on the Sabbath?
back: That the Sabbath was instituted by God for mankind's benefit and refreshment, not to burden people with regulations; and that, since it was ordained for human well-being rather than as an end in itself, humanity's Lord and Representative is authorised to be the official arbiter of how it should be observed.
excerpt:
That the Sabbath was instituted (by God) for mankind's benefit and refreshment Not 
that people were to be made to keep burdensome regulations pertaining to it.

subject: NT
front: For what two reasons did Jesus choose the Twelve?
back: So that they could be with Him, and to be sent out by Him to preach and to have authority to drive out demons.
excerpt: To be sent out by Him to preach, and to have authority to drive out demons (vs. 14-15).

subject: NT
front: What is the sin against the Holy Spirit, according to the syllabus?
back: An attitude of defiant hostility towards God that rejects His saving power expressed in the Spirit-empowered person and work of Jesus - a person's preference for darkness though exposed to light, which can harden into a condition in which repentance and forgiveness become impossible.
excerpt: This refers to an attitude of defiant hostility towards God that rejects His saving power towards man, expressed in the Spirit empowered person and work of Jesus.

subject: NT
front: Which four acts of divine power are related in Mark 4:35 - 5:43?
back: The calming of a violent storm; the healing of a demoniac; the raising of the daughter of Jairus; and the healing of the woman with an issue of blood.
excerpt: From 4:35 to 5:43 are related four acts of divine power wrought by Jesus in a situation of human helplessness and despair:

subject: NT
front: To what did Jesus attribute the cure of the woman with the issue of blood, and what did the address 'Daughter' signify?
back: The cure was attributed to her faith rather than to the touch of His clothing; the address 'Daughter' suggested her new relationship with Him, and 'Go in peace and be healed' assured her that the healing was complete and permanent.
excerpt: The cure was also attributed to her faith rather than the touch of His clothing.

subject: NT
front: Why did the Twelve anoint the sick with oil?
back: Both because of its medicinal properties and for its symbolic value, indicating that the disciples acted by Jesus' authority and power and not their own; it is also to be thought of as an accessory to miraculous healing and a stimulus to faith.
excerpt:
The anointing with the oil was both because of its medicinal properties (cf. Lk. 10:34; James 
5:14) and its symbolic value indicating that the disciples acted by Jesus' authority and 
power, not their own.

subject: NT
front: How is the threefold ministry of the Twelve summarised in Mark 6:12-13?
back: Preaching repentance, driving out demons and healing the sick - showing that Jesus' power extended beyond His personal presence.
excerpt: The threefold ministry of the Twelve is summarized as preaching repentance, driving out demons and healing the sick.

subject: NT
front: Why did Jesus call the religious leaders 'hypocrites', quoting Isaiah 29:13?
back: Because they made an outward profession of worshipping God but gave Him no genuine worship from their hearts.
excerpt: They were "hypocrites" because they made an outward profession of worshipping God but gave Him no genuine worship from their hearts.

subject: NT
front: Why did Jesus use saliva, touch and an upward look in healing the deaf and dumb man?
back: He used sign language and symbolic acts suited to the man's needs, to awaken faith by encouraging him to expect healing; being deaf, the man could not hear a vocal prayer, so by looking up to heaven Jesus indicated that He was praying.
excerpt: He used saliva (v. 31), touching also the ears and tongue, apparently to awaken in the man faith by encouraging him to expect healing.

subject: NT
front: What was the leaven of the Pharisees, and what was the leaven of Herod?
back: From Luke 12:1 we learn that the leaven of the Pharisees was hypocrisy; the leaven of Herod was irreligion, and the leaven of bread was probably worldliness and sensuality. In context the yeast referred to a gradual increase of unbelief.
excerpt: We learn from Luke 12:1 that leaven of the Pharisees was hypocrisy; the leaven of bread

subject: NT
topic: From Galilee to Jerusalem: Jesus Concentrates on Ministry to His Disciples
front: Where are the three predictions of the passion found in Mark?
back: Mark 8:31, 9:31 and 10:33; from Peter's confession onwards the narrative is dominated by the thought of the approaching passion.
excerpt: The narrative, from this point is dominated by the thought of the approaching passion, of which there are three definite predictions. (8:31; 9:31; 10:33)

subject: NT
front: What does it mean to deny oneself and take up one's cross, according to Mark 8:34?
back: To abandon the attitude of self-centredness, and to take up one's own (not His) cross - in other words, to be prepared to die.
excerpt: Any person who enlisted in His cause would need to deny himself (v. 34) that is, abandon the attitude of self- centeredness, and take up his own (not His) cross, in other words be prepared to die.

subject: NT
front: What did Jesus say the essence of greatness is, when the disciples argued about who was the greatest?
back: That it lay in performing acts of service for other people; He illustrated servant-leadership by taking a child in His arms, one who represented the lowliest disciple.
excerpt: Jesus told them that the essence of greatness lay in performing acts of service for other people (v. 35, also 10:43-44).

subject: NT
front: What did Jesus mean by saying 'the kingdom of God belongs to such as these' when the children were brought to Him?
back: That the kingdom belongs to people who, though not literally children, are imbued with such childlike characteristics as trust and receptiveness; it is not gained by human achievement or merit but must be received as God's gift through simple trust.
excerpt: God's kingdom is not gained by human achievement or merit; it must be received as God's gift through simple trust by those who acknowledge their inability to gain it any other way.

subject: NT
topic: The Beginnings of Conflict with the Religious Leaders (vs. 12-12:44)
front: What had the Court of the Gentiles become, and why was Jesus outraged?
back: The high priest Caiaphas had authorised a market there for ritually pure items, and the merchants and money changers turned it into a bazaar, making it impossible for any Gentile to use the area for prayer; Jesus was outraged by this disregard for the area set apart for Gentile use, since the temple was intended as a house of prayer for all nations.
excerpt: In it the High priest Caiaphas had authorized a market for the sale of ritually pure items necessary for temple sacrifice: wine, oil, salt, approved sacrificial animals and birds.

subject: NT
front: Why was the question about paying the poll tax to Caesar a trap, and how did Jesus answer it?
back: To insist on payment would alienate the people; to deny its legitimacy would allow Him to be reported to Rome as a rebel. Jesus replied that since the money bore the Emperor's image it was Caesar's property and the tax should be paid, adding that they should give back to God what is God's.
excerpt: Obviously the question was designed to place Jesus in a religious and political dilemma.

subject: NT
front: What suggestions does the syllabus offer for why Judas betrayed Jesus?
back: That Judas, the only non-Galilean of the Twelve, may have responded to the official orders to report Jesus' whereabouts; that he was disillusioned by Jesus' failure to establish a political kingdom; and that his love for money moved him. What is clear is that he came under satanic control.
excerpt: Judas, the only non-Galilean member of the Twelve, may have responded to the official

subject: NT
front: Who wrote the Book of Acts, and what does Paul call him?
back: Luke, a medical officer and companion of Paul, whom Paul calls 'Our dear friend Luke, the doctor' (Col. 4:14) and a colleague (Philemon 24); it can be inferred that he was Greek.
excerpt: Paul refers to him as "Our dear friend Luke, the doctor" (Col. 4:14) and as a colleague (Philemon 24).

subject: NT
front: What theological purpose does Acts serve?
back: It gives guidance to the church on how to live until Jesus comes again, and on how to transmit the gospel to people who had never seen Jesus in the flesh.
excerpt: In terms of its theology, Acts gives guidance to the church on how to live until Jesus comes again and on how to transmit the gospel to people who had never seen Jesus in the flesh.

subject: NT
front: What two qualifications were required of the candidates for the twelfth apostleship?
back: They must be well-known members of the apostolic band, associated with them during the ministry of Jesus; and they must be witnesses to His resurrection.
excerpt: They must be well-known members of the apostolic band, associated with them during the ministry of Jesus.

subject: NT
front: How does the syllabus define the Ascension?
back: The withdrawal of Jesus from our vision but not from the world.
excerpt: The Ascension is the withdrawal of Jesus from our vision but not from the world (Mt. 28:20).

subject: NT
front: How does Pentecostal glossolalia differ from the spiritual gift of 1 Corinthians 14?
back: The Pentecostal tongue-speaking is apparently different; the 1 Corinthians account of tongue-speaking is to be used in private and public worship, and with caution and restraint.
excerpt: This Pentecostal glossolalia (tongue speaking) is apparently different from the spiritual gift in 1 Corinthians 14.

subject: NT
front: Which verse is called the church's birthday description, and what four things did the believers devote themselves to?
back: Acts 2:42 - they devoted themselves continually to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.
excerpt:
"And they were continually devoting 
themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to 
prayer" (v. 42).

subject: NT
front: Which are the three miraculous jail releases in Acts?
back: The release of the apostles in Acts 5, of Peter in Acts 12:6-10, and of Paul and Silas in Acts 16:26-27.
excerpt: In Acts this is the first of three miraculous jail releases (cf. Peter, 12:6-10; Paul and Silas, 16:26-27).

subject: NT
front: Who were the two most prominent members of 'the seven' appointed to represent the Hellenists?
back: Stephen, who had a grasp of the universal character of the Gospel and became a key figure in early Christian history; and Philip, who carried the Gospel to Samaria and West Judea.
excerpt: One other prominent member of the "seven" was Philip who carried the Gospel to Samaria and West Judea.

subject: NT
front: What did Stephen's face like the face of an angel signify?
back: It was exactly what happened to Moses' face when he came down from Mount Sinai with the Law, apparently showing that both Moses' ministry of the Law and Stephen's interpretation of it have God's approval.
excerpt: This is exactly what happened to Moses' face when he came down from Mount Sinai with the Law (Ex. 34:29).

subject: NT
front: What is the relation between the names Saul and Paul?
back: Saul is the Hebrew name and Paul the Greek name of the same person; his conversion marked a significant turning point in the missionary agenda of the church.
excerpt: Saul is the Hebrew name and Paul the Greek name of the same person.

subject: NT
topic: THE BEGINNING OF THE GENTILE MISSION - LEADERSHIP OF PETER (9:32-12:25)
front: Who was Dorcas, and what did Peter do at Joppa?
back: A well-beloved Christian woman and disciple of Joppa, known for her help to the poor. When she died Peter came from Lydda, prayed and commanded her to get up; to avoid ceremonial defilement he apparently did not touch her until after God restored her to life.
excerpt: While Peter was at Lydda, a well-beloved Christian woman (a disciple) in Joppa, called Dorcas, died. She was known for her help to the poor.

subject: NT
front: Where were the disciples first called Christians?
back: At Antioch, which became the springboard for mission to the Gentile world.
excerpt: Significantly, the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch.

subject: NT
front: For what reasons was Barnabas a wise choice to be sent to Antioch?
back: He was a Levite who, like some of the Christian ambassadors, came from Cyprus; he was a generous person and therefore thoughtful of others; and he was gracious, as his nickname 'Son of encouragement' attests. Luke sums him up as 'a good man, and full of the Holy Spirit and of faith'.
excerpt: He was a gracious person, attested to by his nick name, "Son of encouragement" (4:36).

subject: NT
front: What did Agabus prophesy, and when did it occur?
back: A great famine. Josephus reports that a great famine occurred in about AD 46 - actually a series of severe famines that struck various sections of the Roman Empire during the reign of Emperor Claudius, AD 41-54.
excerpt: (Josephus reports that a great famine occurred in about AD 46. These were actually a series of severe famines that struck various sections of the Roman Empire during the reign of Emperor Claudius - AD 41-54.)

subject: NT
front: What change of centre and of leadership took place from Acts 13 onwards?
back: Jerusalem was still the mother church, but Antioch became the missionary church and Saul's headquarters; Peter was no longer the central figure, for Saul had become the central figure. From Antioch he started his journeys, and to Antioch he returned to report.
excerpt: Jerusalem was still the mother church, but the missionary church was Antioch. Peter was no longer the central figure, Saul had become the central figure.

subject: NT
front: How is the ministry of the Holy Spirit seen in the call to Macedonia?
